passage:
Monday, statistics lecture. The professor wrote a formula on the board and moved on. Elizabeth frowned at the squared term, then raised her hand. "Sorry, why do we square the differences instead of just adding them up?" A few heads turned. The professor smiled and drew a number line, showing how the positives and negatives would cancel each other out. Two rows behind, someone whispered, "Oh, that's why."
Thursday, tutorial. Sahil had nodded through Monday's lecture and now stared at problem three, copying steps from his notes without knowing what they were for. He turned the page and said nothing.
The next Tuesday, quiz. Elizabeth finished the variance question in four lines. Sahil left a gap. At the door afterwards he caught up with her. "Can you show me the squared bit? I never got it." She pulled out a pen and started on the back of his notes.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth ask the professor on Monday?
qa.a: She asked why the differences are squared instead of just added up.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling when he nodded through the lecture and later stayed quiet over problem three?
qa.a: He seems embarrassed and unsure. Copying steps he did not understand and saying nothing suggests he did not want to look behind the others.

qa.q: What turning point helped Sahil start catching up?
qa.a: He admitted at the door that he never understood the squared part and asked Elizabeth to show him. Saying so out loud gave him something real to work from.

qa.q: How might the classmates two rows behind have felt when Elizabeth asked her question?
qa.a: Relieved. One whispered "Oh, that's why," which suggests they were confused too and were glad someone else asked.

grounding: A student who asks a basic question openly learns faster than one who nods along and hides confusion.

Sir just picked up the chalk and worked one small example, twice. By the end of the month I was explaining it to others. Meera kept nodding until the first test, and then she came to me, red in the face, and asked me to teach her. I did, and we both passed.

qa.q: Which subject did Zainab study in her first year?
qa.a: Zainab studied commerce, and spent a week on debit and credit without knowing which was which.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling as she asked her question in front of the class?
qa.a: Zainab was nervous. The cold hands and the giggles around show it took courage, but Zainab asked anyway.

qa.q: What choice did Zainab make on Friday that changed her month?
qa.a: Zainab said out loud that the answer was not known instead of nodding along. That let sir explain from the beginning.

qa.q: Why did Meera finally ask Zainab for help?
qa.a: After the first test, nodding had clearly not taught Meera anything. She was embarrassed, as her red face shows, but ready to admit it. 🤍

grounding: An elder recalls that admitting not knowing in class led to faster learning than for a classmate who kept nodding.

passage:
I'm Samir, and I sit two desks from Sudha. Last Thursday her report was praised in the team meeting. "Oh, it's nothing," she said, waving a hand. "Honestly, I'm hopeless with these things, anyone could have done it." Then she looked around the table and waited. Two colleagues jumped in with "No, no, it was great." She smiled and said, "You're too kind."
She says some version of this most weeks. Afterwards she checks her phone, and I've seen her reread the group thread for replies. I can't know what she feels. Maybe she really doubts herself. But I've started to feel awkward, not sure whether to praise her again or stay quiet, and today I stayed quiet.

qa.q: What did Sudha say when her report was praised?
qa.a: She said it was nothing and that she was hopeless with these things and anyone could have done it.

qa.q: What is Samir feeling while watching Sudha's pattern repeat?
qa.a: Samir feels awkward and unsure whether to give more praise or stay quiet. That is why Samir stayed silent today.

qa.q: What could Samir try instead of adding to the praise or staying silent?
qa.a: Samir could name one specific thing liked in the report and then ask what Sudha found hard about it. That gives a real conversation without feeding a routine.

qa.q: What might Sudha want when she says she is hopeless and then looks around the table?
qa.a: She may want reassurance or recognition. Waiting and rereading the thread suggest she hopes for more praise, though Samir cannot be sure of her inner state.

grounding: A colleague notices someone say she is nothing while seeming to wait for praise.

qa.a: He said he was nothing, just lucky, and that Rafiq did the real work.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling by the third time Sachin said he was nothing?
qa.a: Rafiq was uneasy and a little wary, having noticed Sachin said it soon after someone walked past and glanced at Rafiq's face each time. Still, Rafiq cared enough to answer differently.

qa.q: What changed when Rafiq answered differently on Monday?
qa.a: Rafiq named something specific and asked an open question. Sachin then admitted a real worry about the spacing, and they worked on it together.

qa.a: Probably surprised, since he blinked and paused. He may have felt caught out, and also relieved to say something true.

passage:
Deepika ran into the courtyard with her cheeks burning. Her wooden bullock cart lay on the mud, one wheel snapped off. "Bhupen! I told you not to touch it!" she shouted. Her little brother was not there. She found him behind the big water pot, curled up, the wheel in both hands, his whole body shaking.
Then she remembered him going silent for a whole day after Baba scolded him for dropping the milk can. His eyes were wide and wet.
"Did you think I would hit you?" she asked, slowly. Bhupen nodded. Deepika took a breath. She was still angry, and the anger tugged at her again when she looked at the cart. But she sat down beside him. "Give me the wheel. We'll ask Dada to fix it."

qa.q: Where did Deepika find Bhupen?
qa.a: She found him behind the big water pot, holding the wheel in both hands.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she found Bhupen and then looked at the cart again?
qa.a: She was still angry, and the anger tugged at her again. But it was mixed with sympathy once she saw how frightened he was.

qa.q: What small step let Deepika stay calm even though she was still angry?
qa.a: She asked him a quiet question and then offered a plan to fix the cart. Taking a breath and sitting beside him gave the anger time to settle.

qa.q: How did Bhupen see Deepika's first shout?
qa.a: As frightening. He hid behind the water pot, shook and had wide wet eyes, which suggests he thought she might hit him.

grounding: A child realises her brother who broke a toy was frightened, not being unkind, though her anger still tugs at her.

Thabo's model plane had taken three weeks to build. Now the left wing lay in two pieces on the living-room floor. "You wrecked it!" Thabo yelled. His hands were shaking with rage. "You never listen, Kaito!"
His younger brother stood very still by the sofa, holding a wet sock in one hand. He had gone pale. He didn't argue, and he didn't leave.
Thabo stopped. Kaito never went quiet like that. "Were you trying to put it back on the shelf?" Thabo asked. Kaito nodded, tears sliding down. "I knocked it. I was scared you'd be angry, so I just stood here."
Thabo's anger flared up again when he saw the wing. He breathed out slowly. "Get the glue. It will still fly, sort of."

qa.q: How long had Thabo's model plane taken to build?
qa.a: It had taken three weeks to build.

qa.q: What was Thabo feeling when he saw the wing and then looked at Kaito?
qa.a: He was furious at first and the anger flared again at the sight of the wing. Seeing Kaito go pale and silent added worry and made him stop.

qa.q: What could Thabo do next to keep the repair from turning into another fight?
qa.a: He could work on the glue job together with Kaito and let his own anger cool first. Giving Kaito a job helps him feel forgiven.

qa.q: What is it like for Kaito to be shouted at over an accident?
qa.a: It is scary and lonely. He did not argue or run, which suggests he felt he deserved it, and he needed to hear he was not being blamed for meanness.

grounding: A child sees that his brother who broke the toy was afraid, and holds onto that view though anger returns.

Manjula slammed the gate so hard the hens scattered. "You don't trust me!" she had shouted, and her father Kunal had said only, "You are not riding to college on the highway after dark, and that's final." In her head, the reasons piled up: every other girl in the village did it, he treated her like glass, he never listened.
She sat on the roof with her arms crossed until the light went orange. Slowly the hot feeling drained out. She remembered last monsoon, when the bus was late and she came off it at eight to find Kunal standing at the stop with a torch and his slippers wet through, saying nothing, just walking beside her home.
That night she carried his tea to the cot. "Baba, I was angry," she said. "Can we talk about the college timings again?"

qa.q: What did Kunal say he would not allow?
qa.a: He said she was not to ride to college on the highway after dark.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling on the roof, and how did it change?
qa.a: She was hot with anger at first, then it drained away. Remembering the torch and wet slippers at the bus stop softened her, and she felt ready to talk.

qa.q: What helped Manjula move from shouting to talking?
qa.a: She waited on the roof until her anger drained, then remembered his waiting for her. Then she asked to talk about the timings and did not restart the fight.

qa.q: How does Kunal probably see Manjula's shouting and slammed gate?
qa.a: He may see it as hurtful, yet still as a young person's frustration. His rule comes from fear, and calm talk later gives him room to listen to her.

passage:
I'm Rohan. Last week Elizabeth's mock results came back and she told everyone at school her life was over, flat, like a fact. On Sunday I went to her house to return a book and found her on the verandah with her grandfather Francis, who was peeling a mango.
I stayed quiet by the gate. Francis told her that at nineteen he had been sacked from a printing press and walked home twelve kilometres with his tools in a sack. "I thought that was the end of me. Then a man at the corner shop needed a hand with his accounts." He kept peeling as he talked.
Elizabeth didn't say anything, but she stopped hugging her knees. I can't tell what she really thought. On Monday, though, she stopped saying "over" and asked me to share my notes.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth's grandfather Francis do at the printing press at nineteen?
qa.a: He was sacked from it and walked home twelve kilometres with his tools in a sack.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth probably feeling before Francis told his story?
qa.a: She was in despair and very worried about the mock results, since she declared her life was over. Her hugged knees suggest she felt small and stuck.

qa.q: What could Elizabeth do next to use what she heard from Francis?
qa.a: She could ask him what he did in the weeks after and then plan one small step for her own exams, such as going through her notes with a friend.

qa.q: How might Francis have felt telling Elizabeth about being sacked?
qa.a: He may have felt a little vulnerable, but calm and caring. He kept peeling the mango and told it plainly, without a lecture, as a way to be near her.

grounding: A grandparent's story of a hard time gives a teenager a longer view of her own trouble, seen by an onlooker.

The next Thursday, Bhavna signed up for the debate club's practice session as an audience member. "Just to watch," she told him. He nodded, and asked nothing else.

Sahil, you look like the world has ended. Let me tell you what happened to me. I'm Farida, and at twenty-one, two days before my final project was due, my laptop died and the only copy went with it. I sat on the hostel stairs shaking. My roommate Uzma sat beside me and asked, "How much will this matter in a year?"

Rain had ripped the tarp off the fest stall at 7:40 am, and the gates opened at 9. Shankar stood in a puddle, holding a sodden banner, his jaw tight. Every poster he had painted for two weeks was smeared. "It's ruined," he said. "Everything's ruined."
Kavitha, stapling a spare cloth to the frame beside him, didn't tell him to calm down. "Okay. In a year, who will remember this?" Shankar laughed shakily. "Me. Probably my parents, because I'll tell them." "And who would have noticed the posters?" "Maybe the first ten people who walk by."
He wiped his face. It still stung. But he picked up the marker and started on a fresh sign with a bigger, simpler design, and by 8:55 it was drying under the cloth.

Nour had not lost an argument in the debate seminar all term. Yuki, who taught it, watched him take apart classmates' points with a grin, and she had noticed other things too. He had spent a week arguing with his landlord over a small deposit charge and won, then lost the room when the landlord refused to renew. Yuki did not say anything else. She packed her bag and told him the seminar hall was hers until five if he wanted to talk.

qa.a: They may admire his skill but also feel steamrolled. Nour's constant winning may make it harder for them to enjoy discussing things with him.

Vinita had been teaching at the village school for three years when an NGO in the district town offered her a job with better pay and no chalk dust. She didn't say yes or no. She walked to Dilnaz's house, a former colleague who had made the same move. "The pay is good," Dilnaz said. "But I miss the children in the mornings. Ask yourself which you'd miss more."

I had two parathas that day. Nobody had told me to do anything. I just thought that my stomach was full and his wasn't. So I walked over and tore one paratha in half. "Want this?" I said.
He looked surprised. "You sure?" I nodded. He ate it fast, then said thanks in a small voice.
I didn't tell anyone. Afterwards I felt light, like when you run and stop. I started looking for who else was sitting alone. I'm Rafiq, and that was the first time I noticed that I liked giving.
